articles.body: Every few weeks someone asks me which motion tool they should standardise on. The honest answer is that they are not the same category of thing, so the comparison people want — "which one wins" — cannot be answered in the abstract. So I ran the same brief through all five. Here is the brief: A product card in a React storefront. Hover lifts it and reveals a quick-add button. Quick-add opens a quantity stepper. Changing quantity springs the price. Adding to cart plays a success state, then a toast. It must work with keyboard focus, respect prefers-reduced-motion , and read its price from live data. That last sentence is what separates the tools. Not the animation.

A ZoomEye count-only query on November 18, 2026 found 1,746 matches for title="FreeScout" and 1,260 for app="FreeScout" . The difference suggests that some deployments can be identified by both fields and others only by title, but the counts still describe indexed services rather than confirmed customer environments. The query used page 1, page size 1 and sub_type=all . Only totals were collected. A result could be a demo, an internal helpdesk or a reverse-proxy page with the product title. It could also miss a customized instance. Treat the count as a starting inventory and keep the exact query and timestamp with any later comparison.

articles.title: Before You Print That App Download QR Code, Test Where It Goes
articles.excerpt: Your designer sends over a QR code for an upcoming app launch. Someone scans it on an iPhone. The App Store opens. Looks good. But what happens on Android? What does a laptop visitor see? And if someo…
articles.body: Your designer sends over a QR code for an upcoming app launch. Someone scans it on an iPhone. The App Store opens. Looks good. But what happens on Android? What does a laptop visitor see? And if someone changes the destination after the artwork has gone to print, will the same QR code still work? A QR code that scans successfully isn't necessarily ready to print. Once it's on 2,000 flyers, correcting a mistake becomes a lot less convenient. QR is only the beginning Let's say your app is available in the App Store and on Google Play. You could print two QR codes, but then you're asking people to figure out which one they need before they even reach the app. Another option is a single public URL with device-aware routing.

articles.title: Why message 50 of your chatbot costs 19x more than message 1
articles.excerpt: You build a chatbot and quote the cost of one short message. The real bill arrives, and it is far higher. The reason is two ideas: tokens, and the context window. Here is the arithmetic. All numbers b…
articles.body: You build a chatbot and quote the cost of one short message. The real bill arrives, and it is far higher. The reason is two ideas: tokens, and the context window. Here is the arithmetic. All numbers below are made up for illustration. What is a token? A model does not read whole words. It reads tokens: a short word, part of a long word, a piece of a number, or a punctuation mark. A tokenizer cuts your text into these pieces before the model sees it. Rule of thumb for English: one token is about four characters, so a 500-word page is roughly 700 tokens. Code, numbers and non-English text need more tokens for the same meaning, so they cost more. Repeated words are counted every time. You pay for both copies.

articles.title: Space is filling up with junk. Could laser-reflecting mirrors help humanity clean things up?
articles.excerpt: The British company Foundational thinks its laser-reflecting tech can help humanity fight the space-junk problem — and it just proved out a demo version in an orbital test.
articles.body: A British startup thinks it can help humanity deal with its space junk problem. Millions of pieces of space debris circle Earth at the moment, according to the European Space Agency (ESA). Even the smallest fragments are potentially dangerous, given how fast stuff travels in orbit. Experts have proposed a range of measures to deal with this junk. The smallest bits, for example, may require big space nets, or lasering the stuff down to Earth. Large satellites are increasingly being deliberately deorbited these days, and a few have even been refueled to keep them operating in orbit — something that will likely start happening more and more over the coming years. Now, the British startup Foundational has another idea to throw into the mix: retroreflectors.

articles.title: Astronomers discover rare black holes that formed when stars failed to go supernova
articles.excerpt: Gravitational waves have revealed a population of black holes that may have been born when masssive stars failed to go supernova.
articles.body: Gravitational waves have revealed a population of black holes that may have been born when masssive stars failed to go supernova. Most of us know the origin story of black holes , or we thought we did. Massive stars run out of the fuel for nuclear fusion and their cores collapse. As this happens, the stars' outer layers expand outwards. Shockwaves from the core collapse strike the outer layers, triggering a supernova explosion. The collapsed core creates a black hole. However, new research based on gravitational wave data collected by LIGO (Laser Interferometer Gravitational-Wave Observatory) and its gravitational wave detector partners, Virgo and KAGRA (Kamioka Gravitational Wave Detector), suggests this might not be the complete picture of black hole birth.

articles.title: ULA lost a Vulcan Centaur rocket carrying 40 Amazon satellites 10 minutes after launch — but the failure began just after liftoff
articles.excerpt: United Launch Alliance's Vulcan Centaur rocket failed during its launch on Sunday (Nov. 15) because of an issue with its first-stage booster, according to the company.
articles.body: The failure of a Vulcan Centaur rocket carrying a full load of internet satellites for Amazon was caused by an anomaly in its first-stage booster, rocket maker United Launch Alliance said today (Nov. 17). That failure — which led to the loss of 40 Amazon Leo internet satellites — was recognized about 10 minutes after liftoff, but the problems began much earlier than that, ULA said in a statement. "While we appear to have lost telemetry and the mission at approximately 10 minutes into flight, early indications are that just after liftoff the launch vehicle experienced low booster performance, resulting in stage separation occurring when the vehicle was low in altitude and below minimal velocity to reach orbit," ULA wrote in today's update .
